
# How to Use Windows 11: Complete Beginner's Guide


## What is this in plain English?


Think back to the 1970s and early 1980s, when using a computer meant typing cryptic commands on a black screen with green text. If you wanted to open a file, you had to memorize and type something like "DIR C:\DOCUMENTS" and then "OPEN LETTER.TXT"—and heaven help you if you made a spelling mistake. There were no pictures, no mouse, no clicking on icons. You needed to learn a programming language just to accomplish basic tasks. Computers were for specialists, hobbyists, and people with technical training.


Windows changed all of that. When Microsoft released Windows in 1985 (and more successfully with Windows 3.0 in 1990), they introduced the idea of a "graphical user interface" or GUI (pronounced "goo-ee"). Instead of typing commands, you could see little pictures (icons) representing programs and files. Instead of memorizing commands, you could move a mouse pointer around the screen and click on what you wanted. Instead of a black screen with text, you had windows (hence the name) that showed your work, just like looking at papers on different parts of your desk.


Windows 11 is Microsoft's latest version of this operating system, released in October 2021. An operating system is the master program that controls your entire computer—it's like the manager of a building who makes sure all the rooms (programs) work properly, the utilities (internet, printers) function correctly, and everything is organized and secure. Windows 11 is what you see when you turn on your computer, what lets you run programs like web browsers and word processors, and what manages all your files, photos, and documents.


If you're used to older versions of Windows (like Windows 7 or Windows 10), Windows 11 will look somewhat different—the Start menu moved to the center of the screen, the corners are more rounded, and many settings are in new locations. If you've never used a computer before, Windows 11 is actually a good place to start because it's designed to be more intuitive and user-friendly than ever before. If you've been using smartphones or tablets, many concepts will feel familiar—touch screens work beautifully, apps install easily, and the interface is clean and modern.


This guide will teach you everything you need to know to use Windows 11 confidently: how to navigate the desktop (the main screen you see), how to open and close programs, how to find and organize your files, how to browse the internet, how to stay safe from viruses and scams, how to personalize your computer to your preferences, and how to troubleshoot common problems. We'll use simple language, provide step-by-step instructions, and relate computer concepts to familiar real-world objects whenever possible (like comparing files to papers in filing cabinets, or programs to appliances in your home).


By the end of this guide, Windows 11 will feel less like a mysterious machine and more like a helpful tool that makes your life easier—whether you're video calling grandchildren, managing finances, writing letters, browsing recipes, shopping online, or simply exploring the internet's vast resources.


## Before You Start: Understanding What Windows 11 Is and What You Need


**What Exactly Is Windows 11?**


**Windows 11 is an operating system**—the fundamental software that makes your computer work.


**Think of it this way:**

- **Your computer's hardware** (the physical machine) is like a car's engine, wheels, and frame
- **Windows 11** is like the car's controls, dashboard, and steering wheel that let you actually drive it
- **Programs/Apps** are like different destinations you can drive to

**Without Windows 11 (or another operating system), your computer is just expensive metal and plastic that does nothing.**


**What Windows 11 Does:**


**It manages everything on your computer:**

- **Displays the screen** you interact with (desktop, menus, icons)
- **Runs programs** (web browser, email, word processor, games)
- **Organizes files** (documents, photos, music, videos)
- **Connects to internet** and manages WiFi
- **Controls hardware** (printer, mouse, keyboard, camera, speakers)
- **Keeps you safe** with built-in security (antivirus, firewall)
- **Handles updates** to keep everything current

**You don't need to understand how it does all this—just how to use it.**


**How Windows 11 Differs from Windows 10:**


**Visual changes:**

- **Start menu centered** (bottom-middle instead of bottom-left)
- **Rounded corners** everywhere (softer, modern look)
- **New icons** (colorful, simplified designs)
- **Redesigned Settings** (easier to find things)
- **Snap Layouts** (organize windows more easily)

**New features:**

- **Widgets** (weather, news, stocks at a glance)
- **Chat integrated** (Microsoft Teams built-in)
- **Android apps** (can run phone apps on computer—somewhat)
- **Better touch support** (if you have touchscreen)
- **DirectStorage** (faster gaming—if you're a gamer)

**If you've used Windows 7 or Windows 10, you'll recognize most concepts but need to learn new locations for familiar features.**


**If you've never used Windows before, Windows 11 is actually easier to learn than older versions.**


**What You Need to Use This Guide:**


**Essential:**

1. **A computer running Windows 11**
    - Desktop or laptop
    - PC (not Mac—Macs use different operating system)
2. **Mouse or touchpad**
    - Desktop: external mouse
    - Laptop: built-in touchpad (or external mouse)
3. **Keyboard**
4. **Monitor/screen** (obviously—you're looking at it)
5. **Power and internet connection**
6. **30-60 minutes for initial learning**
7. **Patience** (learning takes time, that's normal)

**Helpful but optional:**
8. **Touchscreen** (some computers have them, most don't—not required)
9. **Printer** (for later, when printing documents)
10. **External storage** (USB drive for backing up files—covered later)


**Basic Computer Parts You Should Know:**


**1. Mouse:**

- **What it is:** Device you move with your hand to control pointer on screen
- **Left button:** Primary button (click to select, open things)
- **Right button:** Secondary button (opens menus with options)
- **Scroll wheel:** Middle wheel (scroll up/down on pages)
- **Pointer/Cursor:** Arrow on screen that moves when you move mouse

**Mouse actions:**

- **Click:** Press left button once quickly
- **Double-click:** Press left button twice quickly (opens programs/files)
- **Right-click:** Press right button once (shows menu of options)
- **Drag:** Hold left button down while moving mouse (moves items)
- **Scroll:** Roll wheel up/down (moves page up/down)

**2. Keyboard:**

- **Letter keys:** Type letters (A-Z)
- **Number keys:** Type numbers (0-9, across top)
- **Enter/Return key:** Confirms action or creates new line
- **Spacebar:** Long key at bottom (adds space between words)
- **Backspace:** Deletes character to left of cursor
- **Delete:** Deletes character to right of cursor
- **Arrow keys:** Move cursor up/down/left/right
- **Shift:** Hold to type CAPITAL LETTERS or symbols above numbers
- **Ctrl (Control):** Used with other keys for shortcuts (like Ctrl+C to copy)
- **Alt:** Used with other keys for menu shortcuts
- **Windows key:** Key with Windows logo (⊞)—opens Start menu

**3. Monitor/Screen:**

- Displays everything
- Shows desktop, programs, files, websites
- You look at this to see what computer is doing

**4. Desktop/Laptop differences:**


**Desktop:**

- **Separate components:** Monitor, keyboard, mouse, tower (computer box)
- **Not portable** (stays in one location)
- **Usually more powerful** for the price
- **Easier to upgrade** (add more memory, storage, etc.)

**Laptop:**

- **All-in-one:** Screen, keyboard, touchpad built into single unit
- **Portable** (battery-powered, take anywhere)
- **More expensive** for same power
- **Harder to upgrade**
- **Touchpad instead of mouse** (built-in, under keyboard)

**Important Terms to Know:**


**Desktop:**

- The main screen you see when computer starts
- Shows wallpaper (background image) and icons
- Like the top of your physical desk where you work

**Icon:**

- Small picture representing program, file, or folder
- Double-click to open
- Think of icons like labeled drawers in a filing cabinet

**Program/App/Application:**

- Software that does specific task
- Examples: Web browser (Chrome, Edge), Word processor (Word), Email (Outlook)
- Think of programs like appliances in your home (each has specific purpose)

**File:**

- Document, photo, video, or any saved data
- Stored on your computer's hard drive
- Like a paper document in filing cabinet

**Folder:**

- Container that holds files or other folders
- Organizes files into categories
- Like a physical folder in filing cabinet

**Window:**

- Rectangular frame that contains program or file
- Can be opened, closed, moved, resized
- Like a framed picture on your wall—can rearrange them

**Taskbar:**

- Bar at bottom of screen
- Shows open programs and system information (time, volume, WiFi)
- Like a quick-access toolbar

**Start Menu:**

- Menu that appears when you click Start button
- Lists programs, recent files, power options
- Your launching point for everything

**Setting Realistic Expectations:**


**What you'll be able to do after this guide:**

- ✓ Navigate Windows 11 confidently
- ✓ Open and close programs
- ✓ Find and organize files
- ✓ Browse the internet safely
- ✓ Customize your desktop
- ✓ Troubleshoot basic problems
- ✓ Perform everyday tasks independently

**What takes more time/practice:**

- ⏳ Advanced file management
- ⏳ Installing and configuring complex software
- ⏳ Troubleshooting hardware problems
- ⏳ Understanding network settings deeply
- ⏳ Mastering keyboard shortcuts

**What this guide won't cover in depth:**

- ✗ Specific programs (Microsoft Word, Excel, etc.)—those need separate guides
- ✗ Hardware repair (broken screens, replacing parts)
- ✗ Advanced networking (setting up servers, complex WiFi issues)
- ✗ Programming or software development
- ✗ Gaming-specific features (unless you're interested)

**Learning Curve Timeline:**


**Day 1:** Basic navigation, opening programs (feels awkward)
**Week 1:** More comfortable, less hunting for things (still referring to guide)
**Month 1:** Confident with daily tasks (occasional questions)
**Month 3:** Windows 11 feels natural (rarely think about it)


**Everyone learns at different pace—this is normal.**


**Common Beginner Fears (and Why They're Unfounded):**


**"I'll break the computer if I click the wrong thing"**

- **Reality:** Very hard to permanently damage computer through software
- Can always restart computer
- Most actions are reversible
- Worst case: restore to earlier state (we'll cover this)

**"I'm too old to learn computers"**

- **Reality:** Age has nothing to do with learning ability
- Millions of seniors use computers daily
- Often easier than you expect
- Patience and practice are what matter

**"I don't speak computer language"**

- **Reality:** You don't need to
- This guide uses plain English
- Technical terms explained when necessary
- Think of it like learning to drive—you don't need to understand the engine

**"Everything changes too fast"**

- **Reality:** Basic concepts stay the same
- Desktop, files, folders—same for 30+ years
- New features usually optional
- Core tasks haven't changed much

**Privacy and Security Note:**


**Windows 11 collects some data** (like all modern operating systems):

- Diagnostic information (error reports, performance data)
- Usage patterns (which features you use)
- Location (if you enable it)

**Why:**

- Improve Windows
- Personalize experience
- Security and updates

**You can control this:**

- Settings → Privacy & Security
- Turn off what you're uncomfortable with
- We'll cover this in detail later

**Most people accept defaults** (Microsoft is reputable company, not selling your personal info like some apps).


**If privacy is major concern:**

- Can disable most data collection
- Reduces some features (like location-based weather)
- But core functionality unchanged

**What to Do If You Get Stuck:**


**This guide is long** (comprehensive, so you have complete resource).


**If overwhelmed:**

1. **Read one section at a time** (don't try to memorize everything)
2. **Practice each section** before moving to next
3. **Bookmark/print for reference** (refer back as needed)
4. **Ask for help** (friends, family, local library computer classes)
5. **Be patient with yourself** (everyone struggles at first)

**Remember: Everyone who uses computers confidently today was once exactly where you are now—confused and uncertain. The only difference is they kept trying.**


**The "You Can't Break It" Reassurance:** One of the biggest barriers to learning computers is fear of making mistakes. Here's the truth: It's almost impossible to permanently damage your computer by clicking the wrong thing in Windows. You won't delete the operating system by accident. You won't erase everything on your hard drive. You won't "break" Windows. The worst that happens? A program closes, a setting changes (you can change it back), or the computer slows down (restart fixes it). Microsoft designed Windows 11 to protect you from yourself. So explore fearlessly. Click around. Try things. If something unexpected happens, you can almost always undo it or restart the computer. This isn't a delicate antique—it's a tool designed to be used.


## Step 1: Turning On Your Computer and Understanding the Desktop


Let's start with the absolute basics: starting your computer and understanding what you see.


**Turning On Your Computer:**


**Desktop Computer:**

1. **Make sure everything is plugged in:**
    - Monitor to power outlet
    - Computer tower to power outlet
    - Monitor to computer tower (video cable—HDMI, DisplayPort, or VGA)
    - Keyboard and mouse to computer (USB or PS/2)
2. **Press power button on computer tower:**
    - Usually on front of tower
    - Large round button, sometimes with power symbol (⏻)
    - Press once, release (don't hold)
3. **Press power button on monitor:**
    - Usually on front or bottom of monitor
    - Press once
    - Some monitors turn on automatically when computer starts

**Laptop:**

1. **Make sure laptop is charged or plugged in:**
    - If battery dead, must plug into power outlet
    - Power light should indicate charging
2. **Open lid** (if closed)
3. **Press power button:**
    - Usually above keyboard or on side
    - Press once, release
    - Some laptops turn on when you open lid

**What Happens When You Turn On Computer:**


**Boot sequence** (computer starting up):

1. **Screen stays black** for 5-30 seconds (computer checking itself)
2. **Manufacturer logo appears** (Dell, HP, Lenovo, etc.) with loading indicator
3. **Windows logo appears** with spinning circle (Windows loading)
4. **Lock screen appears** (shows time, date, maybe photo)

**This takes 30 seconds to 2 minutes** depending on computer age and speed.


**First-time setup:**

- If brand new computer, Windows asks setup questions
- Choose language, region, connect to WiFi, create account
- Follow on-screen prompts
- Takes 10-30 minutes
- **Be patient**—lots of "preparing" and "setting up" messages

**The Lock Screen:**


**What you see:**

- Large photo (scenic image usually)
- Time and date
- Maybe weather, calendar events
- "Press any key to continue" (bottom of screen)

**What to do:**

1. **Press any key** on keyboard (Spacebar easiest)
    - OR click anywhere with mouse
    - OR swipe up (if touchscreen)
2. **Login screen appears**

**The Login Screen:**


**What you see:**

- Your profile picture (or generic icon)
- Your username
- Password field
- "Sign in" button

**How to log in:**

1. **Click in password field** (if not already selected)
2. **Type your password:**
    - Carefully (case-sensitive: "Password" ≠ "password")
    - You'll see dots instead of letters (security feature)
    - If you make mistake, use Backspace to delete and retype
3. **Press Enter** or **click "Sign in"**
4. **Wait for Windows to load** your profile (10-30 seconds)
    - "Welcome" message appears
    - Desktop loads

**If you forget password:**

- Click "I forgot my password" link
- Answer security questions OR
- Use password reset email (if set up)
- Worst case: Need administrator help or computer reset

**The Desktop (Your Home Base):**


**After logging in, you see the Desktop.**


**What the Desktop is:**

- Main screen you work from
- Like the top of your physical desk
- Home base—return here between tasks

**Desktop components:**


**1. Wallpaper (background image):**

- Large photo covering entire screen
- Usually scenic/abstract image
- Purely decorative (customize later if you want)

**2. Desktop icons (optional):**

- Small pictures with labels
- Usually at left side or top-left of screen
- Common ones:
    - **This PC** (access drives, folders, files)
    - **Recycle Bin** (deleted files go here temporarily)
    - **User folder** (your documents, photos, etc.)
    - **Program shortcuts** (quick access to programs)

**3. Taskbar (bottom bar):**

- Solid bar across bottom of screen
- Most important navigation tool
- Contains several sections:

**Taskbar components (left to right):**


**a. Start button** (Windows logo, center-left or far left):

- Click to open Start menu
- Access all programs and settings
- Your main launching point

**b. Search icon** (magnifying glass, next to Start):

- Click to search computer
- Find files, programs, settings
- Type what you're looking for

**c. Task View** (overlapping rectangles icon):

- Shows all open windows at once
- Switch between programs easily
- Create virtual desktops (advanced)

**d. Pinned app icons** (middle section):

- Programs you use frequently
- Click once to open
- Examples: Edge (browser), File Explorer, Microsoft Store
- Can customize which apps appear here

**e. System tray** (far right):

- Small icons showing system status:
    - **WiFi/Network** (connected to internet?)
    - **Volume** (speaker icon—sound level)
    - **Battery** (laptops—how much charge left)
    - **Language** (ENG = English)
    - **Date and Time** (click for calendar)
    - **Notifications** (bell icon—alerts and messages)
    - **Show hidden icons** (^—expands to show more icons)

**4. Widgets button** (weather/news icon, left side of taskbar):

- Opens slide-out panel
- Shows weather, news, stocks, calendar
- Optional feature (can ignore)

**Understanding the Mouse Pointer:**


**What it is:**

- Arrow (↖) on screen that moves when you move mouse
- Sometimes changes shape:
    - **Arrow** (↖): Normal selection
    - **Hand** (👆): Clickable link
    - **I-beam** (I): Text you can edit
    - **Spinning circle** (⌛): Computer is busy/thinking
    - **Resize arrows** (↔ ↕ ⤡): Can resize window

**Mouse pointer can't disappear**—if you lose it:

- Move mouse around (pointer will appear somewhere)
- Or press Ctrl key (makes pointer flash in Windows 11)

**Your First Actions on Desktop:**


**Practice these basic mouse actions:**


**Click:**

1. **Point at Start button** (Windows logo on taskbar)
2. **Press left mouse button once quickly**
3. **Start menu opens**
4. **Click elsewhere** (anywhere on desktop) to close menu

**Right-click:**

1. **Right-click on empty area of desktop** (press right mouse button)
2. **Context menu appears** (list of options)
3. **Click elsewhere** to close menu
4. **This works almost everywhere** (right-click shows options for whatever you're pointing at)

**Double-click:**

1. **If you have "This PC" icon** on desktop
2. **Point at it**
3. **Click left button twice very quickly** (this is a double-click)
4. **Window opens** showing your drives
5. **Click X** (top-right) to close window

**Drag:**

1. **Point at desktop icon** (like Recycle Bin)
2. **Hold down left button**
3. **Move mouse** (icon moves with it—you're dragging it)
4. **Release button** (icon stays where you dropped it)
5. **Practice moving icon around desktop**

**If double-click doesn't work:**

- You're clicking too slowly (practice faster)
- Or double-click speed set very fast (we can adjust later)

**Desktop Right-Click Menu:**


**Right-click on empty desktop area** to see options:

- **View:** Change icon size, arrange icons
- **Sort by:** Organize icons by name, date, size, type
- **Refresh:** Reload desktop (rarely needed)
- **Personalize:** Change wallpaper, colors, themes (covered later)
- **Display settings:** Monitor resolution, multiple displays
- **New:** Create new folder, shortcut, file

**Exploring these options won't break anything—click around to see what they do.**


**Understanding Windows (the rectangular frames):**


**A "window" is a rectangular frame** containing program or folder contents.


**Window components:**


**1. Title bar** (top of window):

- Shows window name
- Shows program icon

**2. Window controls** (top-right corner, three buttons):

- **Minimize** (—): Hides window to taskbar (doesn't close, still running)
- **Maximize/Restore** (⬜ or ⧉): Fullscreen or windowed
- **Close** (✕): Closes window completely (quits program)

**3. Menu bar or Ribbon** (below title bar):

- Contains tools and commands
- Different for each program

**4. Content area** (main part of window):

- Shows program content, files, web page, etc.

**5. Scroll bars** (right side and/or bottom):

- If content bigger than window
- Drag scroll bar to see more
- Or use mouse scroll wheel

**6. Status bar** (bottom of window):

- Shows information about current state
- Number of items, zoom level, etc.

**Window actions:**


**Move window:**

- Point at title bar
- Drag to move window around screen

**Resize window:**

- Point at edge or corner of window
- Pointer changes to resize arrows (↔ ↕ ⤡)
- Drag to make window larger or smaller

**Maximize window:**

- Click maximize button (⬜)
- Window fills entire screen
- OR double-click title bar (same result)

**Minimize window:**

- Click minimize button (—)
- Window hides to taskbar
- Click taskbar icon to bring back

**Close window:**

- Click X button
- Window closes completely
- Unsaved work may prompt "Save first?"

**Practice opening and closing windows:**

1. **Click Start button** (Windows logo on taskbar)
2. **Click "Settings"** (gear icon)
3. **Settings window opens**
4. **Practice:**
    - Minimize window (— button)
    - Click Settings icon on taskbar (window returns)
    - Maximize window (⬜ button)
    - Restore window (⧉ button—same location)
    - Drag title bar to move window
    - Drag corner to resize window
5. **Close window** (✕ button) when done practicing

**Shutting Down Your Computer:**


**At end of day (or when finished):**


**Proper shutdown:**

1. **Click Start button** (Windows logo)
2. **Click Power button** (⏻ icon, bottom-right of Start menu)
3. **Choose option:**
    - **Shut down:** Turns off completely (most common)
    - **Restart:** Turns off and back on (do this if computer acting strange)
    - **Sleep:** Low-power mode, wakes up quickly (laptops often use this)

**Wait for computer to shut down completely:**

- Screen goes black
- Lights turn off
- Fans stop
- Takes 10-30 seconds

**Don't unplug or hold power button** unless computer frozen/unresponsive.


**Sleep vs Shutdown:**


**Sleep:**

- Low-power state
- Work saved in memory
- Wakes up in 2-5 seconds
- Good for short breaks (hours)
- Laptops: Uses some battery

**Shutdown:**

- Completely off
- No power used
- Starts fresh on boot
- Takes 30-120 seconds to start
- Good for end of day, travel

**Most people:**

- **Sleep** during day between uses
- **Shutdown** at night

**What If Computer Won't Turn On:**


**Troubleshooting:**

1. **Check power:**
    - Plugged into outlet?
    - Outlet working? (test with lamp)
    - Power button on power strip turned on?
2. **Check connections:**
    - Power cable firmly connected to computer?
    - Monitor cable connected to computer?
3. **Monitor on?**
    - Separate power button for monitor
    - Check monitor power light
4. **Laptop charged?**
    - Plug into power, wait 5 minutes, try again
5. **Press and hold power button** for 10 seconds (force shutdown)
    - Wait 10 seconds
    - Press power button normally
    - Computer should start

**If still doesn't work:**

- Hardware problem (need tech support)

**Desktop Keyboard Shortcuts (Optional, but Helpful):**


**These shortcuts do things faster than mouse:**

- **Windows key (⊞):** Opens Start menu
- **Windows + D:** Show desktop (minimizes all windows)
- **Windows + L:** Lock computer (requires password to return)
- **Alt + Tab:** Switch between open programs
- **Alt + F4:** Close current window
- **Ctrl + C:** Copy selected item
- **Ctrl + V:** Paste copied item
- **Ctrl + Z:** Undo last action

**Don't memorize now**—use mouse until comfortable, then gradually learn shortcuts.


**The Desktop as Your Workshop:** Think of your computer's desktop like a woodworker's workbench or a kitchen counter. It's your main work surface. The taskbar at the bottom is like a tool belt—everything you need frequently is right there. Icons on the desktop are like tools you use sometimes but not constantly (so you keep them on a shelf within reach). Programs that are running are like projects you're working on—they take up space on your workbench (windows on screen), and when you're done, you put them away (close windows). This mental model helps: Desktop = workspace, Taskbar = quick access tools, Windows = active projects.


## Step 2: Using the Start Menu and Opening Programs


The Start menu is your command center—let's learn to navigate it.


**Opening the Start Menu:**


**Three ways to open Start menu:**


**Method 1: Click Start button**

- Click Windows logo (center-left of taskbar, or far left depending on settings)
- Start menu pops up

**Method 2: Press Windows key**

- On keyboard, press key with Windows logo (⊞)
- Usually bottom-left of keyboard, near Ctrl
- Same result as clicking

**Method 3: Right-click Start button** (advanced)

- Right-click Windows logo
- Shows power user menu (different from regular Start menu)
- Has advanced options
- Ignore for now

**Understanding the Start Menu Layout:**


**When Start menu opens, you see:**


**Top section: Pinned Apps**

- Grid of program icons with names
- Programs you use frequently
- Click any icon to open that program
- Labeled "Pinned" at top

**Middle section: Recommended**

- Recently used files and programs
- Windows suggests things you might want to open
- Labeled "Recommended"

**Bottom section: Footer**

- **Your profile icon** (left): Account settings
- **Power button** (right): Shutdown, restart, sleep

**Search bar (very top):**

- "Search for apps, settings, files, and more"
- Type anything to search entire computer
- Most powerful feature (we'll use extensively)

**Opening a Program from Start Menu:**


**Example: Opening Microsoft Edge (web browser)**

1. **Click Start button** (or press Windows key)
2. **Look at Pinned apps section:**
    - See "Microsoft Edge" icon? (blue/green wave icon)
    - Click it once
    - Edge opens in new window
3. **If you don't see it:**
    - Click "All apps" (button at top-right of Pinned section)
    - Alphabetical list of all programs appears
    - Scroll down to "Microsoft Edge"
    - Click it

**The program opens in its own window.**


**Viewing All Installed Programs:**


**To see complete list of programs:**

1. **Open Start menu**
2. **Click "All apps"** (top-right of Pinned section)
3. **Alphabetical list appears:**
    - Scroll up/down to browse
    - Programs organized A-Z
    - Some grouped in folders (like "Microsoft Office")

**Opening program from All Apps:**

- Click program name
- Program opens

**Going back to Pinned view:**

- Click "Back" button (top-left)

**Using Search to Find Programs (Easiest Method):**


**Search is fastest way to find anything:**


**Example: Opening Notepad (simple text editor)**

1. **Click Start button**
2. **Click in search box** (top of Start menu)
3. **Start typing:** "notepad"
    - As you type, results appear below
    - After typing "note" you'll probably see Notepad
4. **Click "Notepad" in results**
    - OR press Enter (opens top result)
5. **Notepad opens**

**Search works for:**

- Programs/apps
- Files and documents
- Settings
- Web results (if not found on computer)

**Search is so powerful, many people rarely use any other method to find things.**


**Common Programs You'll Use:**


**Here are programs included with Windows 11:**


**Microsoft Edge:**

- Web browser (explore internet)
- Blue/green wave icon
- Like Internet Explorer from old Windows (Edge replaced it)

**File Explorer:**

- Browse files and folders on computer
- Yellow folder icon
- Like Windows Explorer in older Windows

**Settings:**

- Configure Windows (wallpaper, WiFi, accounts, etc.)
- Gear icon
- Replaces Control Panel from older Windows (though Control Panel still accessible)

**Microsoft Store:**

- Download new apps and programs
- Shopping bag icon
- Like Apple App Store or Google Play Store

**Notepad:**

- Simple text editor
- For plain text notes, quick lists
- No formatting (no bold, colors, fonts)

**Paint:**

- Simple drawing program
- Create or edit images
- Basic but fun

**Photos:**

- View and organize photos
- Basic editing (crop, rotate, adjust brightness)

**Calculator:**

- Standard/scientific calculator
- Handy for quick math

**Mail:**

- Email program
- If you set up email account

**Calendar:**

- Track appointments and events

**Clock:**

- World clock, timer, stopwatch, alarms

**Weather:**

- Current conditions and forecast
- Based on your location

**News:**

- Curated news articles
- Personalized to interests

**These are free with Windows 11—installed automatically.**


**Pinning and Unpinning Programs:**


**"Pinning" means adding program to Start menu or taskbar for quick access.**


**To pin program to Start menu:**

1. **Find program** (in All Apps list or via search)
2. **Right-click program name**
3. **Select "Pin to Start"**
4. **Program icon appears** in Pinned section of Start menu

**To unpin:**

1. **Right-click program icon** in Start menu
2. **Select "Unpin from Start"**
3. **Icon removed** (program still installed, just not pinned)

**To pin to taskbar:**

1. **Right-click program** (in Start menu or All Apps)
2. **Select "Pin to taskbar"**
3. **Icon appears on taskbar** (always visible, even when Start menu closed)
4. **Click icon to open program** anytime

**To unpin from taskbar:**

1. **Right-click icon on taskbar**
2. **Select "Unpin from taskbar"**

**Pin programs you use daily** (email, web browser, etc.) **to taskbar or Start menu for easy access.**


**Organizing Start Menu:**


**Rearrange pinned apps:**

1. **Open Start menu**
2. **Click and drag app icon** to new position
3. **Release** (icon stays in new location)
4. **Create groups** by positioning related apps near each other

**Create folders in Start menu:**

1. **Drag one app icon onto another**
2. **Folder created** containing both apps
3. **Click folder** to expand
4. **Name folder** by clicking "Name folder" and typing (like "Office Apps")

**Resizing Start Menu:**

- Not directly resizable in Windows 11
- Fixed size
- Can customize which apps pinned, but size stays same

**Using Recently Opened Files:**


**"Recommended" section shows recent files:**

1. **Open Start menu**
2. **Scroll down to "Recommended" section**
3. **See recently opened documents, websites, folders**
4. **Click any item** to reopen it

**Useful for quickly returning to work you were doing.**


**Closing Programs:**


**Three ways to close program:**


**Method 1: Click X button**

- Top-right corner of program window
- Closes program completely

**Method 2: File menu → Exit**

- Many programs have File menu
- Click File → Exit (or Quit)
- Same as clicking X

**Method 3: Alt + F4**

- Press Alt and F4 keys simultaneously
- Closes current window/program
- Keyboard shortcut

**If program asks "Save changes?":**

- **Yes:** Saves your work, then closes
- **No:** Discards changes, closes
- **Cancel:** Doesn't close (returns to program)

**Programs running in background:**

- Some programs minimize to system tray (far-right of taskbar)
- Icon appears near clock
- Still running even though window closed
- Right-click icon → Exit to fully close

**Managing Multiple Open Programs:**


**Switching between programs:**


**Method 1: Click taskbar icon**

- Open programs show on taskbar
- Click icon to bring that window to front

**Method 2: Alt + Tab**

- Hold Alt key, press Tab
- Thumbnail images of open windows appear
- Press Tab repeatedly (while holding Alt) to cycle through
- Release keys when desired window highlighted
- That window comes to front

**Method 3: Task View**

- Click Task View icon on taskbar (overlapping rectangles)
- All open windows displayed as thumbnails
- Click desired window

**Windows 11 shows open programs with underline under their taskbar icon.**


**Installing New Programs:**


**Two ways to install programs:**


**Method 1: Microsoft Store (safest, easiest)**

1. **Open Microsoft Store** (Start menu → Microsoft Store)
2. **Browse or search** for program (like "Spotify," "Netflix," "Adobe Photoshop")
3. **Click program**
4. **Click "Get" or "Install"** (or price if paid program)
5. **Program downloads and installs automatically**
6. **Click "Open"** when installation complete

**Apps from Microsoft Store:**

- Verified safe (Microsoft scans for viruses)
- Automatically update
- Easy to uninstall
- Recommended for beginners

**Method 2: Download from website (traditional)**

1. **Visit program's official website** (example: google.com/chrome for Chrome browser)
2. **Click "Download" button**
3. **File downloads** (usually to Downloads folder)
4. **Click downloaded file** to run installer
5. **Follow installation prompts** (click Next, Accept, Install, etc.)
6. **Program installs**

**Only download from official websites** (avoid viruses/malware).


**Uninstalling Programs:**


**If you no longer want a program:**

1. **Right-click Start button**
2. **Select "Installed apps"** (or "Apps and Features")
3. **List of all installed programs** appears
4. **Scroll to find program** you want to remove
5. **Click three dots (⋯)** next to program name
6. **Select "Uninstall"**
7. **Confirm** by clicking "Uninstall" again
8. **Program removed** from computer

**Or:**

- Right-click program in Start menu
- Select "Uninstall"
- Confirm

**Uninstalling frees up disk space and declutters computer.**


**Customizing Start Menu:**


**Change which apps appear:**

- Pin frequently used apps
- Unpin apps you don't use
- Organize into logical groups

**Disable Recommendations section:**

1. **Settings → Personalization → Start**
2. **Toggle "Show recommendations"** to Off
3. **Recommended section disappears** from Start menu

**Number of pinned apps:**

- Settings → Personalization → Start
- Choose "More pins" or "More recommendations"
- Adjusts balance between sections

**The Search Superpower:** The single most valuable skill in Windows 11 is using Search effectively. Instead of memorizing where settings are located or hunting through menus, just click Start and type what you want: "bluetooth" finds Bluetooth settings, "volume" finds volume controls, "uninstall" finds program removal, "firefox" finds and opens Firefox. Search finds programs, files, settings, and even searches the web if it doesn't find a local result. Master this one skill and you'll navigate Windows 11 faster than people who've used it for years. Click Start, type what you want, press Enter. That's it.


## Step 3: Understanding Files, Folders, and File Explorer


Let's learn how Windows organizes your documents, photos, and files.


**What Are Files and Folders?**


**Files:**

- **Digital version of documents, photos, videos, music, etc.**
- Everything saved on computer is a file
- Examples:
    - Word document (.docx)
    - Photo (.jpg, .png)
    - Video (.mp4, .avi)
    - Music (.mp3)
    - PDF document (.pdf)
    - Spreadsheet (.xlsx)

**Think of files as individual papers or photos.**


**Folders:**

- **Containers that hold files** (or other folders)
- Organize files into categories
- Examples:
    - "Vacation Photos" folder holds vacation pictures
    - "Tax Documents 2024" folder holds tax-related files
    - "Recipes" folder holds recipe documents

**Think of folders as manila folders in a filing cabinet.**


**File Explorer (Your Filing System):**


**File Explorer is the program that shows your files and folders.**


**Opening File Explorer:**


**Three ways:**


**Method 1: Taskbar icon**

- Yellow folder icon on taskbar
- Click once
- File Explorer opens

**Method 2: Start menu**

- Click Start
- Type "File Explorer"
- Click result
- OR scroll All Apps to "File Explorer"

**Method 3: Keyboard shortcut**

- Press **Windows key + E** (hold Windows, press E)
- Fastest method
- Memorize this if you use files frequently

**File Explorer Window Layout:**


**When File Explorer opens, you see:**


**1. Title bar** (top):

- Shows current folder name
- Standard window controls (minimize, maximize, close)

**2. Toolbar/Command bar:**

- Buttons for common actions: New folder, Copy, Delete, etc.
- Changes based on what's selected

**3. Address bar:**

- Shows current location (which folder you're viewing)
- Example: This PC > Documents > Tax Documents 2024
- Each level separated by >
- Can click any level to go back to that folder

**4. Search box:**

- Right side of address bar
- Search within current folder
- Type filename to find

**5. Navigation pane** (left side):

- Quick access to important locations
- Sections:
    - **Favorites/Quick Access:** Frequently used folders
    - **This PC:** All drives and main folders
    - **OneDrive:** Cloud storage (if enabled)
    - **Network:** Other computers (if on network)

**6. Main content area** (center):

- Shows files and folders in current location
- Can be displayed as icons, list, details, etc.

**7. Status bar** (bottom):

- Shows number of items in folder
- How many items selected
- Total size of selected items

**Understanding "This PC":**


**"This PC" shows all storage on your computer:**


**Folders:**

- **Desktop:** Everything on your desktop
- **Documents:** Word docs, PDFs, text files
- **Downloads:** Files downloaded from internet
- **Pictures:** Photos and images
- **Music:** Audio files, playlists
- **Videos:** Video files, movies

**Drives:**

- **Local Disk (C:):** Main hard drive (where Windows and programs installed)
- **Other drives:** D:, E:, etc. (additional hard drives, USB drives, DVD drives)

**Click any folder to see what's inside.**


**Navigating Folders:**


**Opening a folder:**

- **Double-click folder icon**
- Contents appear in main area
- Address bar updates showing new location

**Going back:**

- **Click back arrow** (top-left, near address bar)
- Returns to previous folder

**Going up one level:**

- **Click up arrow** (next to back arrow)
- Goes to parent folder
- Example: In Documents > Taxes, up arrow goes to Documents

**Going to specific location:**

- **Click level in address bar**
- Example: Click "Documents" in "This PC > Documents > Taxes" to jump to Documents

**Home button:**

- **Returns to Home view** (default File Explorer starting point)

**Creating Folders:**


**Why create folders:**

- Organize files logically
- Find things easier later
- Group related documents

**How to create folder:**

1. **Navigate to location** where you want folder (example: Documents)
2. **Click "New" button** on toolbar
3. **Select "Folder"**
4. **New folder appears** with name highlighted ("New folder")
5. **Type name** for folder (example: "Recipes")
6. **Press Enter**
7. **Folder created**

**OR:**

- Right-click empty space in folder
- New → Folder
- Name it

**Folder naming tips:**

- Use descriptive names ("Tax Documents 2024" not "Stuff")
- Avoid special characters (\ / : * ? " < > |)
- Keep names reasonable length
- Can use spaces ("My Recipes" is fine)

**Copying, Moving, and Deleting Files:**


**Selecting files:**


**Select one file:**

- Click file once (file highlights)

**Select multiple files:**

- **Consecutive:** Click first file, hold Shift, click last file (all in between selected)
- **Non-consecutive:** Click first file, hold Ctrl, click additional files one by one
- **All files:** Ctrl + A (selects everything in current folder)

**Copying files:**


**Method 1: Right-click**

1. Select file(s)
2. Right-click selection
3. Choose "Copy"
4. Navigate to destination folder
5. Right-click empty space
6. Choose "Paste"
7. File(s) copied to new location (original stays in old location)

**Method 2: Keyboard shortcuts**

1. Select file(s)
2. Press Ctrl + C (copy)
3. Navigate to destination
4. Press Ctrl + V (paste)

**Method 3: Drag with Ctrl**

1. Select file(s)
2. Hold Ctrl key
3. Drag file(s) to destination folder (in navigation pane)
4. Release mouse, then release Ctrl
5. File copied

**Moving files:**


**Move = relocate file (removes from original location)**


**Method 1: Cut and paste**

1. Select file(s)
2. Right-click → "Cut" (or Ctrl + X)
3. Navigate to destination
4. Right-click → "Paste" (or Ctrl + V)
5. File moves to new location, disappears from old

**Method 2: Drag**

1. Select file(s)
2. Drag to destination folder (in navigation pane or another File Explorer window)
3. Release
4. File moves (on same drive)
5. NOTE: Dragging between different drives COPIES instead of moves (unless you hold Shift while dragging)

**Deleting files:**


**Delete = send to Recycle Bin** (can recover if mistake)

1. Select file(s)
2. Press Delete key (on keyboard)
3. OR right-click → "Delete"
4. File moves to Recycle Bin

**Permanent delete:**

- Select file(s)
- Press Shift + Delete
- Confirms "Permanently delete?"
- Click Yes
- File gone forever (can't recover)
- **Use carefully**

**Recycle Bin:**

- Holds deleted files temporarily
- Double-click Recycle Bin icon (desktop) to view contents
- Right-click file → "Restore" to return to original location
- Right-click Recycle Bin → "Empty Recycle Bin" to permanently delete everything
- Files in Recycle Bin still take up disk space until emptied

**Renaming Files and Folders:**


**Three ways to rename:**


**Method 1:**

1. Click file once (select it)
2. Click name again (slowly—not a double-click)
3. Name becomes editable
4. Type new name
5. Press Enter

**Method 2:**

1. Right-click file
2. Select "Rename"
3. Type new name
4. Press Enter

**Method 3:**

1. Select file
2. Press F2 key
3. Type new name
4. Press Enter

**Renaming tips:**

- Can rename file without changing extension (.docx, .jpg, etc.)
- If you delete extension accidentally, file won't open properly
- Windows usually hides extensions (safer for beginners)
- If it warns "Changing file extension may make file unusable," click No and try again without changing part after the dot

**Searching for Files:**


**Can't remember where you saved something?**


**Search in File Explorer:**

1. **Open File Explorer**
2. **Click in search box** (top-right)
3. **Type filename or keywords**
    - Example: "tax return" finds files with those words
4. **Press Enter**
5. **Results appear**
6. **Double-click to open** file

**Search searches current folder and all subfolders.**


**To search entire computer:**

- Navigate to "This PC" first
- Then search
- Searches everywhere (slow but thorough)

**File Types and Extensions:**


**Files have different types** (indicated by icons and extensions):


**Common file types:**


**Documents:**

- **.docx:** Microsoft Word document
- **.pdf:** PDF (Adobe Acrobat) document
- **.txt:** Plain text file
- **.xlsx:** Microsoft Excel spreadsheet
- **.pptx:** Microsoft PowerPoint presentation

**Images:**

- **.jpg / .jpeg:** Photo (most common)
- **.png:** Image with transparency support
- **.gif:** Animated image
- **.bmp:** Bitmap image (large file size)

**Video:**

- **.mp4:** Video (most common)
- **.avi:** Video (older format)
- **.mov:** QuickTime video
- **.wmv:** Windows Media Video

**Audio:**

- **.mp3:** Music (most common)
- **.wav:** Uncompressed audio (large)
- **.wma:** Windows Media Audio
- **.m4a:** AAC audio

**Other:**

- **.zip:** Compressed/archived files
- **.exe:** Program/application (executable)
- **.html:** Webpage

**Each file type opens in specific program:**

- .docx opens in Microsoft Word (or WordPad)
- .jpg opens in Photos app
- .mp3 opens in Windows Media Player (or Groove Music)
- .pdf opens in Microsoft Edge (or Adobe Acrobat Reader)

**Changing default program for file type:**

1. Right-click file
2. "Open with" → "Choose another app"
3. Select desired program
4. Check "Always use this app to open [file type] files"
5. Click OK

**Viewing Files in Different Ways:**


**Change how files displayed:**


**View options** (toolbar button or View menu):


**Extra Large Icons:**

- Large thumbnails
- Good for photos (can see preview)
- Takes up lots of space

**Large/Medium/Small Icons:**

- Icon sizes
- Balance between preview and space

**List:**

- Simple list of names
- Compact
- No preview

**Details:**

- Shows name, date modified, type, size
- Columns you can sort by
- Most informative
- Best for documents

**Content:**

- Mix of icons and details
- Good all-purpose view

**To change view:**

- Click "View" button on toolbar
- Select desired view from menu

**Sorting and Filtering:**


**Sort files by:**

- Name (A-Z or Z-A)
- Date modified (newest first or oldest first)
- Type (groups by file type)
- Size (largest first or smallest first)

**To sort:**

1. **In Details view:** Click column header (Name, Date modified, Type, Size)
2. **In other views:** Right-click empty space → Sort by → Choose option

**Each click toggles ascending/descending order.**


**Filter files:**

- In Details view, click dropdown arrow in column header
- Check/uncheck items to show/hide
- Example: Show only .jpg files, hide others

**File Properties:**


**Every file has properties** (details about the file):


**To view properties:**

1. Right-click file
2. Select "Properties"
3. Window opens showing:
    - **General tab:** Type, location, size, dates (created, modified, accessed)
    - **Details tab:** Additional metadata (for photos: camera model, resolution, date taken; for music: artist, album, track number)
    - **Security tab:** Permissions (who can access)
    - **Previous Versions tab:** Older versions of file (if backup enabled)

**Click OK to close properties window.**


**Properties useful for:**

- Checking file size before emailing
- Seeing when file was last modified
- Finding photo metadata (date taken, camera used)
- Troubleshooting file access problems

**Quick Access:**


**Quick Access shows frequently/recently used folders:**


**Located in left navigation pane** (top section)


**Folders automatically added** based on usage


**To pin folder to Quick Access:**

1. Right-click folder
2. Select "Pin to Quick Access"
3. Folder permanently appears in Quick Access section

**To unpin:**

1. Right-click folder in Quick Access
2. Select "Unpin from Quick Access"

**Customize Quick Access:**

- Only pin folders you use daily
- Keeps navigation pane uncluttered
- Easy access to important locations

**Understanding Drives and Storage:**


**This PC shows drives:**


**Local Disk (C:):**

- Main hard drive
- Contains Windows, programs, your files
- Typically 100-500 GB in size
- Used space shown in red/blue bar

**Other drives:**

- D:, E:, F:, etc.
- Additional hard drives (internal or external)
- USB flash drives
- DVD/CD drives
- Network drives

**To see drive space:**

- Open This PC
- Each drive shows used/total space
- Right-click drive → Properties for detailed breakdown

**If C: drive nearly full:**

- Run Disk Cleanup (see Step 9)
- Delete unnecessary files
- Uninstall unused programs
- Move files to external drive

**Libraries (Advanced Organizational Feature):**


**Libraries are virtual folders** combining multiple locations:


**Default libraries:**

- Documents Library: Shows Documents folder + other locations you add
- Pictures Library: Shows Pictures folder + other locations
- Music Library: Shows Music folder + other locations
- Videos Library: Shows Videos folder + other locations

**Benefits:**

- View files from multiple locations in one place
- Organize without moving files
- Advanced feature—beginners can ignore

**If you see "Libraries" in navigation pane, you can use them. If not, you don't need them.**


**The Filing Cabinet Analogy:** Think of your computer's file system exactly like a filing cabinet in an office. This PC is the entire filing cabinet. Each drive (C:, D:, etc.) is a drawer. Folders are manila folders within those drawers. Files are individual papers inside those manila folders. Just like you wouldn't throw all your papers into a drawer without organizing them, you shouldn't save everything to Desktop or Documents without creating logical folders. Make folders like "Taxes," "Recipes," "Family Photos," "Medical Records"—whatever categories make sense to you. Then save files into appropriate folders. Future you will be grateful when you can find that document quickly instead of searching through hundreds of files.


## Step 4: Browsing the Internet Safely


Let's explore the web using Microsoft Edge browser.


**What Is a Web Browser?**


**A web browser is a program that displays websites.**


**Think of it like:**

- TV that shows different channels (websites)
- Window you look through to see the internet
- Library card that gives you access to millions of books (web pages)

**Microsoft Edge:**

- Default web browser in Windows 11
- Built into Windows
- Fast, secure, modern
- Replaces Internet Explorer from older Windows

**Alternatives:**

- Google Chrome (most popular worldwide)
- Mozilla Firefox (privacy-focused)
- Brave (blocks ads by default)
- Opera (built-in VPN)

**This guide focuses on Edge** (already installed, works well).


**Opening Microsoft Edge:**


**Three ways:**


**Method 1: Taskbar**

- Click Edge icon (blue/green wave, usually pinned to taskbar)
- If not there, see Method 2

**Method 2: Start menu**

- Click Start
- Type "Edge"
- Click Microsoft Edge

**Method 3: Desktop shortcut**

- If Edge shortcut on desktop, double-click it

**Edge opens showing home page** (usually customizable news feed or blank page).


**Understanding the Edge Window:**


**Address bar** (top center):

- Where you type website addresses (URLs)
- Also serves as search bar
- Example: Type "youtube.com" or "weather forecast"

**Tabs** (top of window):

- Each tab = different website
- Can have many websites open simultaneously
- Switch between tabs by clicking them
- Like having multiple books open to different pages

**Back/Forward buttons** (top-left):

- **Back arrow (←):** Go to previous page
- **Forward arrow (→):** Go to next page (after going back)

**Refresh button** (circular arrow):

- Reload current page
- Useful if page doesn't load properly

**Home button** (house icon):

- Returns to home page
- May need to enable in settings

**Favorites button** (star icon):

- Save bookmarks to favorite websites
- Access saved bookmarks

**Collections button** (folder icon):

- Save and organize content
- Advanced feature

**Settings button** (three dots ⋯, top-right):

- Browser settings and options
- Print, zoom, history, etc.

**Profile icon** (top-right corner):

- Your Microsoft account
- Sync across devices
- Sign in/out

**Visiting a Website:**


**Method 1: Type web address (URL)**


**What is a URL?**

- Web address (like street address for building)
- Examples:
    - [www.google.com](http://www.google.com/)
    - youtube.com
    - amazon.com
    - nytimes.com

**To visit website:**

1. **Click in address bar** (top of window)
    - Existing URL highlights
2. **Type website address**
    - Can omit "www" (just type "google.com")
    - Can omit "https://" (Edge adds automatically)
    - Example: Just type "amazon.com"
3. **Press Enter**
4. **Website loads**

**Common URLs to try:**

- **google.com:** Search engine
- **youtube.com:** Videos
- **weather.com:** Weather forecast
- **amazon.com:** Shopping
- **wikipedia.org:** Encyclopedia
- **nytimes.com:** News
- **facebook.com:** Social media (requires account)

**Method 2: Use search**


**You can search directly from address bar:**

1. **Click in address bar**
2. **Type what you're looking for** (not a web address, but a search term)
    - Example: "chocolate chip cookie recipe"
    - Example: "what is the capital of France"
    - Example: "nearby restaurants"
3. **Press Enter**
4. **Search results appear** (from Bing search engine by default)
5. **Click any result** to visit that website

**Search is often easier than remembering exact website addresses.**


**Navigating Web Pages:**


**Scrolling:**

- **Mouse wheel:** Roll up/down to move page up/down
- **Scroll bar:** Drag slider on right side of window
- **Arrow keys:** Up/Down arrows on keyboard
- **Spacebar:** Scrolls down one screenful
- **Page Up/Page Down keys:** Jump up/down by screen

**Clicking links:**

- **Links** (hyperlinks) are colored, underlined text or images
- **Pointer changes to hand** when hovering over link
- **Click link** to go to that page
- **Right-click link** for options:
    - Open link in new tab
    - Open link in new window
    - Copy link
    - Save link

**Most websites:**

- Logo (top-left) links to home page (click to return to start)
- Menu/navigation bar (top) links to major sections
- Footer (bottom) has additional links (contact, privacy policy, etc.)

**Using Multiple Tabs:**


**Tabs let you have many websites open simultaneously.**


**Opening new tab:**


**Method 1: Click + button**

- Click **+** next to last tab (top of window)
- New blank tab opens

**Method 2: Keyboard shortcut**

- Press **Ctrl + T**
- Faster method

**Method 3: Right-click link**

- Right-click any link on page
- Select "Open link in new tab"
- Link opens in new tab without leaving current page

**Switching between tabs:**

- **Click tab** you want to view
- That tab comes to front

**Closing tab:**

- **Click X** on tab (appears when you hover over it)
- OR press **Ctrl + W** (closes current tab)

**Reordering tabs:**

- **Drag tab left or right** to rearrange
- Organize tabs logically

**Practical tip:** Keep related tabs together (all shopping sites in one area, all news sites in another, etc.)


**Bookmarking Favorite Websites:**


**Bookmarks** (also called Favorites in Edge) **save websites for easy access later.**


**To bookmark current page:**


**Method 1:**

1. Click **star icon** in address bar
2. **"Add this page to favorites"** dialog appears
3. **Name:** Edit bookmark name if desired (shorter is better)
4. **Folder:** Choose where to save (Favorites bar, Other favorites, or create new folder)
5. Click **Done**
6. **Bookmark saved**

**Method 2: Keyboard shortcut**

- Press **Ctrl + D**
- Same dialog appears
- Faster method

**Accessing bookmarks:**


**Favorites bar** (if enabled):

- Shows below address bar
- Quick access to most-used sites
- Click any bookmark to visit
- To enable: Settings (⋯) → Favorites → Show favorites bar → Always

**Favorites menu:**

1. Click **star icon** (or **Ctrl + Shift + O**)
2. List of all bookmarks appears
3. Click any bookmark to visit
4. Organized by folders

**Organizing bookmarks:**

1. Click star icon → **three dots (⋯)** → **Manage favorites**
2. List of all bookmarks with options
3. **Drag to rearrange**
4. **Right-click to rename, delete, or move to folder**
5. **Click "Add folder"** to create new folder for organization

**Bookmark frequently visited sites** (news sites, email, banking, weather, etc.) **for one-click access.**


**Searching the Web Effectively:**


**Google is most popular search engine** (others: Bing, DuckDuckGo, Yahoo).


**To use Google:**

1. Visit **google.com**
2. Type search terms in search box
3. Press Enter
4. Results appear

**OR:**

- Type search directly in Edge address bar
- Uses Bing by default
- Can change to Google in settings

**Search tips:**


**Be specific:**

- ❌ "recipe" (too broad)
- ✓ "easy chocolate chip cookie recipe" (specific)

**Use quotes for exact phrases:**

- "windows 11 tutorial" (finds that exact phrase)

**Exclude words with minus:**

- jaguar -car (finds jaguar animal, not car)

**Search within site:**

- site:nytimes.com election news (searches only New York Times)

**Use question format:**

- "how to tie a tie"
- "what is the weather today"
- "when is thanksgiving 2024"

**Google often answers directly** (shows definition, calculation, weather, etc.) **without needing to click results.**


**Recognizing Legitimate vs Scam Websites:**


**Internet has many scams—learn to spot them.**


**Signs of legitimate website:**


**✓ HTTPS and padlock:**

- Address starts with **https://** (not http://)
- **Padlock icon** appears in address bar
- Means connection is encrypted/secure
- Essential for banking, shopping, entering passwords

**✓ Correct URL:**

- Double-check spelling
- amazon.com ✓
- arnazon.com ✗ (imposter)
- Scammers use similar-looking URLs

**✓ Professional design:**

- Clean layout
- Proper grammar and spelling
- Working links
- Contact information

**✓ Known/trusted brand:**

- Major companies: Amazon, Google, Microsoft, banks
- Verified by reputation

**Signs of scam/suspicious website:**


**✗ No HTTPS/padlock:**

- http:// only (not https://)
- No padlock icon
- Don't enter personal information

**✗ Misspelled URL:**

- paypa1.com (number 1 instead of letter L)
- micros0ft.com (zero instead of O)
- Very subtle differences

**✗ Urgent/threatening language:**

- "Your account will be closed!"
- "Click now or lose access!"
- "You've won a prize!"
- Legitimate sites don't use scare tactics

**✗ Too good to be true:**

- "iPhone for $100!"
- "You won $1,000,000!"
- "Work from home, make $5,000/week!"
- If it sounds impossible, it is

**✗ Poor grammar/spelling:**

- Legitimate companies proofread
- Scammers often have errors

**✗ Requests for unusual payment:**

- Gift cards (iTunes, Google Play)
- Wire transfer
- Cryptocurrency
- Legitimate businesses use credit cards, checks

**✗ Unsolicited emails with links:**

- "Your package couldn't be delivered" (you didn't order anything)
- "Your account is suspended" (click to verify)
- Don't click links in unexpected emails
- Visit site directly by typing URL

**If in doubt, don't enter personal information, don't pay, and close the website.**


**Safe Online Shopping:**


**Tips for shopping online safely:**


**1. Shop known retailers:**

- Amazon, Target, Walmart, Best Buy, major brands
- Established reputation
- Customer protection

**2. Check URL before entering payment:**

- Address bar shows **https://** and padlock
- URL is correct (amazon.com, not arnazon.com)

**3. Use credit card (not debit):**

- Credit cards have fraud protection
- Easier to dispute charges
- Debit card uses your actual money (harder to recover)

**4. Save confirmation:**

- Print or save order confirmation
- Screenshot order number
- In case of disputes

**5. Check reviews:**

- Read product reviews
- Check seller ratings (if third-party seller)
- Too many 5-star reviews can be fake (look for detailed reviews)

**6. Compare prices:**

- Visit multiple sites
- Google "[product name] price"
- Make sure "deal" is actually good

**7. Understand return policy:**

- Read return policy before buying
- Know time limit for returns (30 days, 60 days, etc.)
- Who pays return shipping?

**Banking Online:**


**Online banking is safe if you follow precautions:**


**1. Access bank directly:**

- Type bank URL yourself (don't click email links)
- Bookmark bank website
- Ensures you're on real site, not phishing copy

**2. Use strong password:**

- Not same as other sites
- Mix of letters, numbers, symbols
- Change if suspicious activity

**3. Enable two-factor authentication:**

- Requires code from phone in addition to password
- Even if password stolen, can't access without phone

**4. Check for HTTPS and padlock:**

- Essential for banking
- Never enter credentials on http:// site

**5. Don't bank on public WiFi:**

- Coffee shop WiFi not secure
- Wait until home or use phone data

**6. Log out when finished:**

- Don't just close browser
- Click "Log Out" or "Sign Out"

**7. Monitor accounts:**

- Check transactions regularly
- Report suspicious activity immediately

**Downloading Files Safely:**


**Sometimes you need to download files** (PDFs, images, programs).


**When download starts:**

1. **Progress appears** in browser (bottom or top)
2. **File saves to Downloads folder** by default
3. **Click file in browser** to open when complete
    - Or click "Show in folder" to see in File Explorer

**Downloaded files location:**

- This PC → Downloads
- Or quick access via File Explorer sidebar

**Safety rules for downloading:**


**✓ Only from trusted sources:**

- Official websites
- Microsoft Store
- Reputable download sites (CNET, FileHippo—though direct from developer better)

**✓ Scan with antivirus** (Windows Security scans automatically, but can manually scan)


**✗ Don't open unknown attachments** in emails


**✗ Don't download cracked/pirated software** (full of viruses)


**✗ Don't download from pop-ups:**

- "Your computer is infected! Download antivirus!"
- "Update Flash Player" (Flash is dead anyway)
- Legitimate software doesn't push downloads via pop-ups

**Clearing Browsing History:**


**Your browser remembers sites you've visited.**


**To clear history:**

1. **Click three dots (⋯)** → **Settings**
2. **Privacy, search, and services**
3. **Clear browsing data** → **Choose what to clear**
4. **Time range:** Choose how far back (Last hour, Last 24 hours, All time, etc.)
5. **Check items to clear:**
    - Browsing history
    - Download history
    - Cookies and site data
    - Cached images and files
6. **Click "Clear now"**
7. **History deleted**

**Or keyboard shortcut: Ctrl + Shift + Delete** (opens clear data dialog)


**Why clear history:**

- Privacy (if sharing computer)
- Free up space
- Fix website loading issues (clearing cache)

**InPrivate Browsing (Private Mode):**


**Private browsing doesn't save history.**


**To open InPrivate window:**

1. Click three dots (⋯)
2. **"New InPrivate window"**
    - OR press **Ctrl + Shift + N**
3. **New window opens** (dark theme, "InPrivate" label)
4. **Browse normally**
5. **When you close window, history not saved**

**InPrivate mode:**

- Doesn't save browsing history
- Doesn't save cookies
- Doesn't save passwords
- Doesn't save form data

**But:**

- Downloads still saved
- Bookmarks you add still saved
- Your employer/ISP can still see activity (not truly anonymous)
- Not a VPN

**Use for:**

- Shopping for gifts (so recipient doesn't see in history)
- Checking email on someone else's computer (won't save password)
- Researching sensitive topics (medical, financial, etc.)

**The Golden Rule of Internet Safety:** If something feels wrong, it probably is. Legitimate companies don't send urgent emails demanding you click links immediately. Real banks don't ask for passwords via email. Actual tech support doesn't call you about viruses (you call them). You didn't win a contest you didn't enter. That Nigerian prince doesn't have money for you. Trust your instincts—if an email, website, or offer seems too urgent, too good, too scary, or too insistent, it's likely a scam. Close it, delete it, move on. The legitimate version (if it exists) will still be there when you visit the real website directly.


## Step 5: Customizing Your Windows 11 Experience


Make Windows 11 look and feel the way you want.


**Changing Desktop Wallpaper (Background Image):**


**Wallpaper is the background image on your desktop.**


**To change wallpaper:**


**Method 1: Settings**

1. **Right-click empty area of desktop**
2. **Select "Personalize"**
3. **Personalization settings open**
4. **Click "Background"**
5. **Choose background type:**
    - **Picture:** Single image
    - **Solid color:** Plain color (no image)
    - **Slideshow:** Rotates through multiple images
6. **For Picture:**
    - **Browse** to choose image from your computer
    - OR select from **Recent images**
    - OR choose from **included Windows images**
7. **Choose fit:** Fill, Fit, Stretch, Tile, Center, Span (how image displays on screen)
8. **Wallpaper changes immediately**

**Method 2: From photo**

1. **Open image** in Photos app
2. **Right-click image**
3. **"Set as" → "Set as desktop background"**
4. **Wallpaper changes to that image**

**Slideshow option:**

- Automatically changes wallpaper every X minutes
- Select folder containing images
- Choose change frequency (1 minute to 1 day)

**Where to find wallpapers:**

- Windows includes many (Settings → Personalization → Background → Browse)
- Your own photos (Documents → Pictures)
- Online sources: unsplash.com, pexels.com (free)
- Bing or Google image search "desktop wallpapers 4k"

**Changing Theme:**


**Theme = wallpaper + colors + sounds + cursor as a package.**


**To browse themes:**

1. **Settings → Personalization → Themes**
2. **Browse available themes**
3. **Click theme to apply**
4. **Desktop, colors, sounds all change** to match theme

**Download more themes:**

- Click "Browse themes" in Microsoft Store
- Free and paid themes available
- Download and install
- Apply from Themes settings

**Themes are quick way to change entire look at once.**


**Changing Accent Color:**


**Accent color affects taskbar, Start menu, window borders.**


**To change color:**

1. **Settings → Personalization → Colors**
2. **Choose color mode:**
    - **Light:** Light backgrounds (easier on eyes in bright rooms)
    - **Dark:** Dark backgrounds (easier on eyes at night, saves battery on OLED screens)
    - **Custom:** Mix (dark apps, light system, or vice versa)
3. **Accent color:**
    - **Automatic:** Windows chooses based on wallpaper
    - **Manual:** Select specific color from palette
4. **Show accent color on:**
    - Start menu and taskbar
    - Title bars and window borders
    - Check boxes to enable

**Dark Mode benefits:**

- Easier on eyes in low light
- Reduces eye strain
- Looks modern and sleek
- May save battery (OLED screens)

**Light Mode benefits:**

- Easier to read in bright rooms
- More traditional appearance
- Better contrast for some users

**Adjusting Display Settings:**


**Screen resolution, brightness, scaling.**


**To access display settings:**

1. **Right-click desktop**
2. **"Display settings"**
3. **Display settings page opens**

**Key settings:**


**Brightness:**

- Slider adjusts screen brightness
- Laptops: Also adjustable via keyboard keys (usually F1/F2 or Fn + arrow keys)
- Brighter = easier to see, uses more battery
- Dimmer = easier on eyes at night, saves battery

**Night light:**

- Reduces blue light in evening (warmer, orange-tinted screen)
- Easier on eyes before bed
- Toggle on/off, or schedule (sunset to sunrise)

**Scale and layout:**

- Makes text and items bigger/smaller
- **100%:** Standard (small text)
- **125%:** Slightly larger (recommended for many users)
- **150%:** Much larger (easier to read)
- Choose based on eyesight and screen size

**Display resolution:**

- **Recommended** setting is usually best
- Higher resolution = sharper but smaller
- Lower resolution = blurrier but larger
- Most users should leave at recommended

**Multiple displays** (if you have two monitors):

- Extend desktop across both
- Mirror (show same on both)
- Use only one
- Rearrange display position

**Customizing Taskbar:**


**Taskbar is the bar at bottom with Start button and icons.**


**To customize taskbar:**

1. **Right-click empty area of taskbar**
2. **"Taskbar settings"**
3. **Taskbar settings page opens**

**Options:**


**Taskbar alignment:**

- **Center** (default in Windows 11): Start button and icons centered
- **Left:** Start button and icons aligned left (like Windows 10)
- Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behaviors → Taskbar alignment

**Pin/unpin apps:**

- **Right-click app icon** on taskbar → "Unpin from taskbar" (remove)
- **Right-click app** in Start menu → "Pin to taskbar" (add)

**Show/hide taskbar icons:**

- Settings → Personalization → Taskbar
- Toggle items on/off:
    - Search
    - Task View
    - Widgets
    - Chat

**System tray icons:**

- Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Other system tray icons
- Toggle which icons appear (network, volume, battery, etc.)

**Auto-hide taskbar:**

- Settings → Personalization → Taskbar → Taskbar behaviors
- "Automatically hide the taskbar"
- Taskbar disappears when not in use (move mouse to bottom to show)
- Gives more screen space

**Taskbar position:**

- Windows 11 taskbar locked to bottom (can't move to top/sides like older Windows)
- Third-party tools can move it (but not officially supported)

**Adjusting Sound Settings:**


**Volume, output device, sound effects.**


**Quick volume adjust:**

- **Click speaker icon** in system tray (bottom-right)
- **Drag slider** to adjust volume
- Or use volume keys on keyboard (if available)

**Detailed sound settings:**

1. **Right-click speaker icon** → **Sound settings**
2. **Sound settings page opens**

**Options:**


**Output device:**

- Choose which speakers/headphones to use
- If multiple devices (external speakers, monitor speakers, Bluetooth headphones)
- Select desired output from dropdown

**Input device:**

- Choose which microphone to use
- Built-in laptop mic, external USB mic, headset mic

**Volume mixer:**

- Adjust volume for each app independently
- System sounds, browser, music player, etc.
- Click "Volume mixer" to access

**Sound scheme:**

- Windows plays sounds for events (startup, error, notification)
- Settings → System → Sound → More sound settings (under Advanced)
- Change sound scheme or disable individual sounds

**Testing audio:**

- Play music or video
- Adjust volume to comfortable level
- Ensure sound comes from intended device

**Muting:**

- Click speaker icon → Click speaker icon in volume popup (instant mute)
- Or keyboard mute key (if available)

**Setting Up Touch Keyboard (Touchscreen Devices):**


**If you have touchscreen:**


**Enable touch keyboard icon on taskbar:**

1. **Right-click taskbar**
2. **Taskbar settings**
3. Toggle "Touch keyboard" to On
4. **Keyboard icon appears** in system tray

**To use touch keyboard:**

- Click keyboard icon in system tray
- On-screen keyboard appears
- Tap keys to type
- Click X to close keyboard

**Keyboard appears automatically** when you tap in text field (if touchscreen).


**Changing Mouse Pointer Size and Color:**


**If pointer hard to see:**

1. **Settings → Accessibility → Mouse pointer and touch**
2. **Pointer size:** Drag slider to make larger
3. **Pointer style:** Choose color scheme:
    - White (default)
    - Black
    - Inverted (reverses colors underneath)
    - Custom color
4. **Pointer preview** shows how it looks
5. **Changes apply immediately**

**Larger, colored pointer much easier to find on screen.**


**Changing Text Size:**


**If text too small system-wide:**

1. **Settings → Accessibility → Text size**
2. **Drag slider** to increase text size
3. **Preview shows sample text**
4. **Click "Apply"**
5. **All text in Windows gets larger**

**Different from display scaling** (this only affects text, not icons/images).


**Narrator and Accessibility Features:**


**Windows has tools for vision/hearing/mobility impairments:**


**Narrator** (screen reader):

- Reads text on screen aloud
- Settings → Accessibility → Narrator
- Toggle on
- Helpful for blind/low-vision users

**Magnifier:**

- Enlarges portion of screen
- Settings → Accessibility → Magnifier
- Toggle on
- Follow mouse or keyboard focus
- Zoom in/out with keyboard shortcuts

**High contrast:**

- Increases contrast for easier reading
- Settings → Accessibility → Contrast themes
- Choose high contrast theme

**Closed captions:**

- Customize appearance of subtitles
- Settings → Accessibility → Captions

**Keyboard/Mouse alternatives:**

- On-Screen Keyboard (type with mouse)
- Speech recognition (control computer with voice)
- Eye tracking (for users who can't use hands)

**Even if not needed now, good to know these exist.**


**Widgets Panel:**


**Widgets show weather, news, stocks, calendar at a glance.**


**To open Widgets:**

- Click Widgets button on taskbar (weather icon, left side)
- OR press **Windows key + W**
- Panel slides out from left

**What's displayed:**

- Weather (current and forecast)
- News (personalized feed)
- Stocks (if you track any)
- Sports scores
- Calendar events
- To Do tasks

**Customizing widgets:**

- Click "Personalize widgets" (bottom of panel)
- Add/remove widgets
- Rearrange by dragging
- Click settings icon on each widget for options

**To hide Widgets button:**

- Right-click taskbar → Taskbar settings
- Toggle "Widgets" to Off

**Widgets useful for quick information** without opening apps.


**Snap Layouts (Window Management):**


**Snap Layouts help organize multiple windows on screen.**


**To use Snap Layouts:**

1. **Hover mouse over maximize button** (⬜) on any window
2. **Grid appears** showing layout options
3. **Click desired layout** (side-by-side, three windows, four windows, etc.)
4. **Window snaps to selected position**
5. **Other open windows shown** to fill remaining space
6. **Click window** to place in other position

**Keyboard shortcuts for snapping:**

- **Windows key + Left arrow:** Snap to left half
- **Windows key + Right arrow:** Snap to right half
- **Windows key + Up arrow:** Maximize
- **Windows key + Down arrow:** Restore or minimize

**Snap Layouts make multitasking easier:**

- Web browser on left, document on right
- Email on left, calendar on right
- Four windows for complex tasks

**Virtual Desktops:**


**Create multiple desktops for different activities.**


**Example use cases:**

- Desktop 1: Work (email, documents, spreadsheets)
- Desktop 2: Personal (social media, music, news)
- Desktop 3: Gaming or hobbies

**To create virtual desktop:**

1. **Click Task View icon** on taskbar (overlapping rectangles)
2. **Click "+ New desktop"** (top of screen)
3. **Second desktop created**
4. **Click desktop to switch**

**To switch between desktops:**

- Click Task View → Click desired desktop
- OR **Ctrl + Windows key + Left/Right arrows**

**To move window between desktops:**

- Open Task View
- Right-click window thumbnail
- "Move to" → Choose desktop

**To close desktop:**

- Open Task View
- Hover over desktop
- Click X

**Windows from closed desktop move to remaining desktop.**


**Virtual desktops keep work organized and reduce clutter.**


**Personalization is Personal:** There's no "right" way to configure Windows 11—it's entirely about your preferences and needs. If you have trouble seeing small text, make it larger. If you prefer dark backgrounds, enable Dark Mode. If you love a particular photo, make it your wallpaper. If the taskbar icons in the center bother you (many Windows 10 users dislike this change), move them to the left. The beauty of Windows is that it adapts to you. Spend 15 minutes exploring Settings → Personalization and Settings → Accessibility. Adjust things until Windows feels comfortable and looks pleasant to you. Your computer should work for you, not vice versa.


## Step 6: Managing User Accounts, Privacy, and Security


Keep your computer secure and your information private.


**Understanding User Accounts:**


**Each person who uses computer can have their own account.**


**Account types:**


**Administrator account:**

- Full control over computer
- Can install programs
- Can change settings
- Can create/delete other accounts
- Can access all files (even other users')

**Standard account:**

- Limited permissions
- Can't install programs (without admin password)
- Can't change system settings
- Can only access own files
- Good for children or shared computers

**Your first account is usually Administrator.**


**Why multiple accounts:**

- Privacy (each person has their own files, desktop, settings)
- Security (limits what children or guests can do)
- Personalization (each person customizes their own experience)

**Viewing Your Account:**

1. **Settings → Accounts**
2. **Your info:**
    - Shows your account name
    - Profile picture
    - Account type (Administrator or Standard)

**Changing account picture:**

- Settings → Accounts → Your info
- "Browse for one" or "Create your look"
- Choose image from computer or take photo with webcam
- Picture appears on lock screen and Start menu

**Creating Additional Accounts:**


**To add another user:**

1. **Settings → Accounts → Family & other users** (or Other users)
2. **Add account** (under "Other users")
3. **Two options:**
    - **Microsoft account:** Email-based account (recommended)
    - **Local account:** No email, no sync (offline account)

**For Microsoft account:**

1. **Enter email address** of person
2. **They'll receive invitation**
3. **They sign in** with existing Microsoft account (or create one)
4. **Account created**

**For local account:**

1. **"I don't have this person's sign-in information"**
2. **"Add a user without a Microsoft account"**
3. **Enter username and password**
4. **Security questions** (for password recovery)
5. **Account created**

**Choosing account type:**

- After creating account, click it → "Change account type"
- Choose Standard or Administrator

**Most family members should have Standard accounts** (safer).


**Switching Between Accounts:**


**To switch users without logging out:**

1. **Click profile icon** (top-right of Start menu)
2. **List of accounts appears**
3. **Click different account**
4. **Enter password** for that account
5. **Switched** (your programs stay running, can switch back later)

**OR:**

- **Windows key + L** (lock computer, shows login screen, can choose different account)

**Removing an Account:**


**To delete user account:**

1. **Settings → Accounts → Family & other users**
2. **Click account to remove**
3. **"Remove"**
4. **Warning: "Delete account and data?"**
    - **Choose:** Delete account and data, or Delete account but keep data
5. **Confirm**
6. **Account removed**

**Be certain before deleting—can't undo easily.**


**Privacy Settings (What Windows Tracks):**


**Windows collects data for various purposes.**


**To control privacy:**

1. **Settings → Privacy & security**
2. **Many options:**

**General:**

- Let apps show personalized ads
- Let websites provide local content
- Let Windows improve Start and search
- Show suggested content in Settings
- **Toggle off** items you're uncomfortable with

**Speech:**

- Online speech recognition
- Enables dictation, Cortana
- **Toggle off** if you don't use these features

**Diagnostics & feedback:**

- How much diagnostic data to send Microsoft
- **Required diagnostic data** (minimum)
- **Optional diagnostic data** (more info, helps improve Windows)
- Choose level you're comfortable with

**Activity history:**

- Tracks which apps/sites you use (for timeline feature)
- **Toggle off** to disable tracking

**Location:**

- Apps can access your location (for weather, maps, etc.)
- **Toggle off** for specific apps or all apps
- Useful for weather, maps
- Not needed for most apps

**Camera:**

- Which apps can access camera
- Toggle off for apps that don't need it
- Prevents spying

**Microphone:**

- Which apps can access microphone
- Toggle off for apps that don't need it

**App permissions (general):**

- Scroll through list of permissions
- Each shows which apps have access
- Toggle off apps that don't need permission

**Most people:**
